title: Multi-Decadal Land-Cover Transitions and Vegetation Condition in a Protected Montane Forest, Ethiopia (2000–2024)
content: Understanding spatiotemporal land-use/land-cover (LULC) dynamics and their impacts on vegetation condition is essential for the management of protected forest ecosystems under increasing anthropogenic pressure. This study evaluates multi-decadal LULC change and associated vegetation dynamics in the Harenna Forest, Bale Mountains National Park (Ethiopia), from 2000 to 2024 using Landsat imagery, Random Forest classification, and NDVI analysis. Classification accuracy ranged from 80.9% to 87.2%, with Kappa coefficients between 0.739 and 0.826, indicating robust and consistent performance across all years. Results reveal progressive forest conversion primarily to smallholder agriculture, accompanied by localized settlement expansion, reflecting edge-driven encroachment within the protected landscape. NDVI analysis shows clear differentiation among LULC classes, with forest areas maintaining significantly higher vegetation greenness than agriculture, settlement, and bare land (p < 0.001). These findings demonstrate that land-cover transitions are associated with measurable declines in vegetation condition, particularly in forest margin zones where conversion intensity is highest. Despite high overall forest persistence, the observed spatial patterns indicate ongoing pressure and gradual landscape modification. By integrating long-term LULC transition analysis with inferential NDVI assessment, this study provides a quantitative framework for monitoring vegetation dynamics and supports evidence-based forest management and conservation strategies in tropical montane ecosystems.
